title: The Social Contract
author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
openingChapterLabel: Book I, Chapter I — Subject of the First Book
openingText:
I mean to inquire if, in the civil order, there can be any sure and legitimate rule of administration, men being taken as they are and laws as they might be. In this inquiry I shall endeavour always to unite what right sanctions with what is prescribed by interest, in order that justice and utility may in no case be divided.

I enter upon my task without proving the importance of the subject. I shall be asked if I am a prince or a legislator, to write on politics. I answer that I am neither, and that is why I do so. If I were a prince or a legislator, I should not waste time in saying what wants doing; I should do it, or hold my peace.

Man is born free; and everywhere he is in chains. One thinks himself the master of others, and still remains a greater slave than they. How did this change come about? I do not know. What can make it legitimate? That question I think I can answer.
about:
The Social Contract is Rousseau's argument that political authority is legitimate only when it springs from the consent of the people governed. The book opens with the famous line: "Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains." Rousseau then argues that legitimate political order can be built by free people who agree together to be ruled — the "general will" — rather than by monarchs claiming divine right or by force.

Published in 1762, the book was banned in France and Geneva immediately. It was central to the intellectual ferment that produced the French Revolution. Rousseau's argument that sovereignty resides in the people is the founding text of modern democratic theory.

angleCards.title: The general will.
angleCards.text: The concept at the heart of the book — and the most contested idea in modern political philosophy. The general will is not majority opinion, not the sum of private desires, not what a representative decides for you. It is what the people would will if they were genuinely thinking as citizens. Track how Rousseau defines it, where it can go wrong, and why it has been used to justify both democracy and totalitarianism.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read The Social Contract as an extended attempt to define the general will — what distinguishes it from mere majority vote or collective self-interest — and to understand why interpreters disagree so sharply about whether it is the foundation of democracy or a licence for authoritarianism.

angleCards.title: Forced to be free.
angleCards.text: Book I's most explosive line: whoever refuses to obey the general will shall be constrained to do so by the whole body — which means nothing other than that he will be forced to be free. It is either the most coherent statement in the book or its most frightening. Rousseau is not being careless here. He is making a precise argument about what freedom actually is — and it does not mean doing whatever you want.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read The Social Contract for its argument about freedom — specifically the paradox that genuine freedom requires submitting to the general will, and that being 'forced to be free' is not a contradiction but the only definition of political liberty that holds up.

angleCards.title: The Lawgiver.
angleCards.text: Book II introduces one of the strangest figures in political philosophy: the Lawgiver, the near-mythical founder who gives a people its laws, then disappears. He cannot use force; he has no authority of his own; he must persuade the people to accept a constitution they cannot yet understand. Rousseau compares him to Moses, Lycurgus, and Calvin. The paradox is that the general will, which is supposed to be self-governing, apparently needs a god-like founder to get started.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace Rousseau's argument about the Lawgiver — the founder who gives a republic its fundamental laws — and to understand why a theory of radical popular sovereignty needs an almost superhuman individual to set it in motion, and what that tension reveals about the theory itself.

angleCards.title: Civil religion.
angleCards.text: Book IV ends with a chapter that shocked Rousseau's contemporaries more than anything else in the book: the argument that every republic needs an official civil religion — a set of social dogmas citizens must profess or be exiled. Not Christianity, not any existing faith, but a civic creed built around the existence of God, the sanctity of the social contract, and the intolerance of intolerance itself. It is the most controversial chapter in an already controversial book.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read The Social Contract's final chapter on civil religion as the logical terminus of the whole argument — the point at which a theory of popular sovereignty confronts the question of what holds a republic together when the general will alone is not enough — and to decide whether Rousseau's answer is coherent or dangerous.

cast.name: The Social Contract
cast.description: The original agreement by which isolated individuals become a political community. Not a historical event — a logical foundation. Each person gives up their natural freedom and receives in return civil liberty, protected by the whole. The contract is unanimous, not majoritarian: it requires everyone, because it creates the very body that can afterwards make binding decisions.

cast.name: The General Will
cast.description: Rousseau's central and most contested concept. The general will is not what people happen to want, nor the sum of private interests, nor a majority vote. It is what the people would will if they were thinking as citizens concerned with the common good. It is always right — but the assembly can be wrong about what it is. That gap is where the book's most dangerous implications live.

cast.name: The Lawgiver
cast.description: A near-mythical figure introduced in Book II — the great legislator who gives a people its fundamental constitution. He has no authority of his own, cannot use force, and cannot reason with a people who cannot yet understand his laws. So he invokes the gods. Rousseau cites Moses, Lycurgus, and Numa as examples. The Lawgiver is both necessary to the theory and an embarrassment to it.

cast.name: The Body Politic
cast.description: When individuals enter the social contract, they create something new: a single moral and collective body — the republic, the state, the sovereign — that has a will, interests, and identity of its own. It is not a fiction or a useful metaphor. For Rousseau, the body politic is as real as any natural person, and its will — the general will — has genuine authority over all its members.

cast.name: Civil Religion
cast.description: Book IV's most explosive argument: every republic needs a civil religion — not Christianity, which divides loyalty between God and state, but a minimal civic creed. Its dogmas are few: God exists, there is a life to come, the just will be rewarded, the wicked punished, the social contract is sacred. Those who refuse to profess it may be exiled; those who profess and then violate it may be put to death.

cast.name: Forced to be Free
cast.description: The most contested phrase in the book. Whoever refuses to obey the general will shall be constrained to do so by the whole body — which means he will be forced to be free. Rousseau is making a precise argument: natural freedom (doing what you want) is not the same as civil freedom (obeying laws you have given yourself). To be forced into the contract is to be forced into the only form of freedom that actually counts.

whyItMatters.title: The Source of Modern Sovereignty
whyItMatters.body: The book argues that legitimate political authority comes from the people, not from kings, gods, or tradition. The principle is so deeply built into modern politics that it now seems obvious. It was not obvious in 1762, and it required arguments like Rousseau's to make it so.

whyItMatters.title: The General Will
whyItMatters.body: Rousseau's concept of the general will — the collective interest of the people, distinct from the sum of individual interests — has been one of the most influential and disputed ideas in political theory. It shaped democracy and was also used to justify Robespierre. The argument is alive in any conversation about what "the people" want.

whyItMatters.title: Freedom and Obligation
whyItMatters.body: Rousseau insists that being subject to law you helped make is not constraint but freedom. The argument is the foundation of modern liberal democracy. Whether it survives close scrutiny is what political philosophy has been arguing about ever since.
